bib.title: Chapter 2. Data and Sampling Distributions (Practical Statistics for Data Scientists)

question: How do random sampling, bias, sampling distributions, the bootstrap, confidence intervals and common probability distributions let data scientists quantify the error in sample estimates?
contributions: Explains why random sampling still matters in big data
Presents the bootstrap as the general way to get standard errors and confidence intervals
Positions the normal, t, binomial, Poisson, exponential and Weibull distributions for data science

results.claim: A 90% bootstrap confidence interval for mean loan-applicant income is shown for a sample of 20 with mean $57,573.
results.setup: Lending Club annual income, sample of 20, 90% bootstrap CI (Fig 2-9)
results.quote: based on a sample of 20 for which the mean was $57,573

results.claim: Bootstrap of the median loan income (R=1000) gives original median 62000, bias about -$70 and standard error of $209.
results.setup: Lending Club loans_income, R package boot, R = 1000, statistic median
results.quote: The original estimate of the median is $62,000.

results.claim: Halving the standard error requires four times the sample size (square-root of n rule).
results.setup: Standard error of a sample statistic, formula s/sqrt(n)
results.quote: in order to reduce the standard error by a factor of 2, the sample size must be increased by a factor of 4

results.claim: Gallup polled 2,000 people and predicted the 1936 election correctly while Literary Digest polled over 10 million and was wrong, due to sample bias.
results.setup: 1936 US presidential poll, Landon vs Roosevelt
results.quote: George Gallup, founder of the Gallup Poll, conducted biweekly polls of just 2,000

results.claim: With 20,000 stadium attendees each tossing a coin 10 times, the chance that somebody gets 10 heads in a row exceeds 99%, versus 1 in 1,000 for one person.
results.setup: Thought experiment illustrating data snooping / vast search effect
results.quote: (more than 99% — it’s 1 minus the probability that nobody gets 10 heads)

results.claim: In a normal distribution 68% of data lies within one SD of the mean and 95% within two.
results.quote: 68% of the data lies within one standard deviation of the mean, and 95% lies within two standard deviations

results.claim: Binomial example: dbinom(x=2, n=5, p=0.1) returns 0.0729.
results.quote: would return 0.0729, the probability of observing exactly x = 2 successes in n = 5

results.claim: pbinom(2, 5, 0.1) returns 0.9914, probability of two or fewer successes.
Gosset began with resampling: samples of 4 from a data set of 3,000 measurements.
results.quote: drawing random samples of 4 from a data set of 3,000

results.claim: Google processes over 1 trillion queries per year against over 150,000 English words: a true big-data (sparse) problem where random sampling does not help.
results.quote: Google processes over 1 trillion queries per year

limits: Authors are not printed in the chapter text; first_author 'Bruce' is from the book's known authorship, not the PDF (bib.authors left empty). Year not printed.
Formulas (standard error s/sqrt(n), t-interval, binomial mean np and variance np(1-p)) are lost in text extraction; only described in words.
The chapter says CLT and t-distribution matter less in data science because the bootstrap is available; the bootstrap does not compensate for a small sample.
Confidence interval does not answer 'probability the true value lies in the interval' (NOTE in Confidence Intervals).
practices: Use random sampling (stratified when subgroups are rare) to reduce bias even in big-data projects (Random Sampling and Sample Bias).
Prefer data quality and representativeness over quantity; use big data only when data is sparse and long-tailed (Size versus Quality).
Guard against the vast search effect with one or more holdout sets and target shuffling (Selection Bias).
Estimate standard error and confidence intervals with the bootstrap rather than relying on CLT formulas (Standard Error, Confidence Intervals).
Do not assume normality for raw data; check with a QQ-plot and treat normality as a last resort (Normal Distribution, Long-Tailed Distributions).
Pick the distribution using domain knowledge, e.g. Poisson for events per time period (Long-Tailed Distributions NOTE).
Split time into segments where the event rate is roughly constant before using Poisson/exponential; use Weibull when rate changes (Poisson and Related Distributions).
Use the bootstrap to explore sample size by varying n (The Bootstrap).

terms.definition: A subset from a larger data set.
The larger data set or idea of a data set.
Dividing the population into strata and randomly sampling from each strata.
A sample that misrepresents the population.
Extensive hunting through data in search of something interesting.
Bias or nonreproducibility resulting from repeated data modeling, or modeling data with large numbers of predictor variables.
extreme observations tend to be followed by more central ones.
The frequency distribution of a sample statistic over many samples or resamples.
The tendency of the sampling distribution to take on a normal shape as sample size rises.
The variability (standard deviation) of a sample statistic over many samples
A sample taken with replacement from an observed data set.
The process of taking repeated samples from observed data; includes both bootstrap and permutation (shuffling) procedures.
The percentage of confidence intervals, constructed in the same way from the same population, expected to contain the statistic of interest.
The result of standardizing an individual data point.
A plot to visualize how close a sample distribution is to a normal distribution.
A parameter that allows the t-distribution to adjust to different sample sizes, statistics, and number of groups.
The rate (per unit of time or space) at which events occur.
A generalized version of the exponential, in which the event rate is allowed to shift over time.
